\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\subsection{What Generalizes}
Four points carry beyond the instance. \emph{Tariffs select schedules; they do not coordinate.} A flat tariff fixes the water operator's pump-hours and leaves their timing to habit; a pass-through tariff aligns timing with the market but not with the site, and it captured \resCapturedPass\% of the gain here only because the site imports at the market price in most hours; charging the internal price itself captured \resCapturedInternal\% because the on/off pump makes ties between equally priced hours generic, and a tariff cannot break them in the site's favor. \emph{Share the settlement, not audited costs.} Because the water operator's controllable costs are fixed by demand up to the granularity of its pumps, a share of the verifiable market settlement plus a fixed fee aligns incentives exactly, with no open books and no cost-allocation dispute; for a net importer the same contract is a share of the site's bill with a rebate. \emph{The right split is a fee, not a share.} Anchoring the fee on the baseline turns any share into a proportional split of the gain, so bargaining is over one number, and the equal split has a focal point. \emph{Coordinate the plan, contract the outcome.} An internal price and a metered schedule, exchanged a few dozen times, compute the jointly optimal schedule and certify how far from optimal it can be; the contract makes the result self-enforcing. Privacy costs $2|\Bset_{\Pset}|T$ numbers per message.

\subsection{Discreteness}
The two-agent LP model of \cite{altawil2026} had no duality gap and a unique best response to the internal price. Both properties fail with on/off pumps, and the case study shows what replaces them. The recovered schedule reaches the integrated optimum within a handful of exchanges, and the certificate the operators can compute from their own data ends at a gap of \resWarmGapPct\% from the marginal-cost start. On this instance the dual function evaluated at the restricted-LP prices lies \resDualityGapPct\% below the integrated cost, so the Lagrangian relaxation has essentially no duality gap and the residual is the price of finite exchanges, quantized prices, and subproblem tolerances; in general the integer commitments can leave a gap that no price closes (Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence}), and the central solver, holding all the data, itself leaves a gap of \resIntegratedGap\%. And the internal price no longer selects a unique schedule: at $\pi^\star$ the water operator is indifferent between several hours of equal price, and it is the energy operator's response to the metered schedule, inside the planning loop, that picks the one the site can serve most cheaply. These are the two places where the planning protocol does work that a price alone cannot do, and they are the reason the protocol is part of coordinated operation rather than a computational convenience.

\subsection{Limitations}
The fixed on-state pump coefficient \eqref{eq:c_calib} is the principal coupling approximation. It keeps the interface linear and metered, but it does not reward operating a pump near its best-efficiency point, and the modeled pump energy is only as accurate as the calibration trajectory; a validated PWL relation between electrical power and the hydraulic operating point is the natural next step, and it would keep the interface linear in the metered load. The hourly discretization can leave the replayed tank slightly below its terminal requirement (Table~\ref{tab:replay}); a reserve margin or a simulation-informed correction of \eqref{eq:w_tank} would close the gap, and all compared schedules would have to share it. A small synthetic water network and a two-bus feeder do not establish scalability, behavior under feeder congestion, or performance on real operator data; the case does show connection congestion, which is where the internal price departs from the market price. The linearized power flow is most defensible near its expansion point. Water quality, leakage, battery wear, pump switching costs, equipment outages, and forecast uncertainty are absent. The contract analysis is deterministic: under uncertainty the transfer shares whatever settlement materializes, and the allocation of risk between the operators becomes a design question in its own right (Remark~\ref{rem:imbalance}).

\subsection{Implementation Prerequisites}
The contract needs only settlement-grade artifacts, the market settlement statement and the pump submeter, but it does need a legal wrapper: a revenue-sharing agreement with $(\varphi,F)$ negotiated once and revisited periodically, and, for a regulated utility, its regulator's approval of market-indexed income. Corollary~\ref{cor:window} bounds where the terms can be, and the equal split gives a focal point; the outcome will reflect bargaining power and outside options. The planning protocol needs an hourly price and load exchange the day before delivery, which existing demand-response interfaces already provide, and it needs each operator to run its own scheduling problem, which the water operator already does under any hourly tariff. None of these barriers is analytic, but they bound where the scheme applies, and the modest scale of the gain argues for keeping the contractual machinery as light as $(\varphi,F)$ allow.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
This paper modeled the day-ahead coordination of two independently managed local operators, a water utility with schedulable pumping and storage and an energy operator whose PV, battery, feeder, and market interface can monetize that flexibility, as a contracting problem while keeping the physics of both networks. The water operator's decisions were constrained by the MILPNet formulation and the energy operator's by the electrical part of the DES model of Morvaj \emph{et al.}; the two met in one metered quantity, the pump load at its supply bus, and their joint optimum was a MILP. Flat, pass-through, and internal-price tariffs proved unable to coordinate: the first fixes only pump-hours, the second the wrong price in export and congested hours, and the third leaves ties and dictates the division. A revenue-sharing contract with a fixed fee coordinated at every share, its proof unaffected by the integer commitments, and anchoring the fee on the baseline bill turned the share into a proportional split of the gain, which for a net-importing site reads as bill sharing with a rebate. A Lagrangian relaxation of the interface let the operators compute the schedule by exchanging only an internal price and a metered load schedule; a bundle master certified the dual bound where subgradient steps could not, and the price was characterized as the site's nodal marginal cost, equal to the purchase price in import hours, the sale price in export hours, and different from both only where the connection or the feeder is at a limit. In the case study coordination was worth \resGain\ per day, \resGainPctBill\% of the pumping bill; the pass-through tariff captured \resCapturedPass\% of it, the contract all of it at every share, and the distributed scheme found the schedule within a few exchanges from the energy operator's own marginal costs while certifying a gap of \resWarmGapPct\%.

Three extensions follow naturally. First, uncertainty: bidding under PV and price uncertainty with imbalance settlement turns the integrated problem into a two-stage stochastic program; the contract's affine structure extends scenario by scenario, but risk allocation between the operators becomes a design question. Second, a flow- and head-dependent pump power model and larger networks with several pump groups and feeder congestion, which enrich $\Qset$ and $\Xset$ and leave the architecture intact. Third, one-to-many coordination: an energy operator contracting simultaneously with water, thermal, and EV-charging flexibility providers, where the hierarchical decompositions of \cite{palomar2006} apply and the contracting layer raises classical questions of rent division among multiple flexibility suppliers.

\appendix[Proofs]
Throughout, $\dt=1$ to lighten notation, $C=-R$ denotes the site's day-ahead cost, $C^\star=-\Pi^\star$, and $C_{\E}(\ell)=-R_{\E}(\ell)$ is the energy operator's least cost of serving a metered load $\ell$.

\subsection{Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:volume}}
Summing \eqref{eq:w_mass} over $n\in\Jset$ and $t\in\Tset$ and \eqref{eq:w_tank} over $k\in\Kset$ and $t\in\Tset$, every link flow that joins two junctions appears once with each sign and cancels; what remains is the flow leaving the reservoirs, the demand, and the net tank inflow, which telescopes to $A_k(h_{k,T}-h^0_k)/\dt_{\mathrm{s}}$. Rearranging gives the identity. Under \eqref{eq:w_tank_terminal} the storage term is nonnegative. At a schedule that no positive electricity price improves, no pump-hour can be removed while keeping the schedule feasible; since removing pump-hours is the only way to reduce the storage term, that term is at its least feasible value for the given number of pump-hours, which is the granularity statement. Pumping energy is $\sum_p\overline{P}_p\sum_tu_{p,t}$, and two feasible schedules can differ in $\sum_tu_{p,t}$ because the flow delivered in an on-hour is the curve flow at the head the pump faces, which depends on the tank level and the network state in that hour. \hfill$\blacksquare$

\subsection{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:tariff}}
(i) With $\tau_t\equiv\bar\tau$ the objective of \eqref{eq:baseline_w} is $\bar\tau\sum_p\overline{P}_p\sum_tu_{p,t}$, a function of the pump-hour counts alone; every schedule with the minimal counts attains it, so all are best responses and the tariff does not distinguish their timing. If $u^\star$ has more pump-hours than the minimum, its bill is strictly larger than the minimum under every $\bar\tau>0$, so it is not a best response. (ii) Under $\tau_t=c^{\mathrm{buy}}_t+\eta$ the objective is $\sum_tc^{\mathrm{buy}}_t\ell_t(u)+\eta\sum_t\ell_t(u)$; on the set of schedules with a given pump-hour count the second term is constant, and across counts it only adds a constant per hour, so best responses minimize $\sum_tc^{\mathrm{buy}}_t\ell_t$ up to that constant. By Proposition~\ref{prop:price}, $\pi^\star_t\le c^{\mathrm{buy}}_t$ with strict inequality in export, idle, and curtailment hours; if $u^\star$ pumps in such an hour, moving that pump-hour to any hour with $c^{\mathrm{buy}}$ no larger and $\pi^\star$ strictly larger, when feasible, does not increase the pass-through bill but increases the internal-price bill, so $u^\star$ need not minimize the former, and it fails to whenever such a move is feasible; in the case study it does. Indifference between hours of equal price is immediate. (iii) If the Lagrangian relaxation of \eqref{eq:c_pumpload} has no duality gap, $(u^\star,\xi^\star)$ minimizes the Lagrangian at $\pi^\star$, so $u^\star$ minimizes $\sum_t\pi^\star_t\ell_t(u)$ over $\Qset$ and is a best response to $\pi^\star+\eta$; any schedule with the same price-weighted load is also a best response, hence ties. Under $\tau=\pi^\star+\eta$ the water operator's payoff is $-\sum_t(\pi^\star_t+\eta)\ell^\star_t$, affine and strictly decreasing in $\eta$, and the energy operator's is $C^\star$ less that bill; the attainable divisions of $\gain$ form the half-open interval of payoffs so generated, which is bounded above by the baseline participation constraint only for $\eta$ in a range that need not intersect the range required by the other operator's constraint. \hfill$\blacksquare$

\subsection{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:contract}}
\emph{$\E$'s side.} Given $u^\star$, $\E$'s payoff is $(1-\varphi)R(\xi)+F$ with $\xi\in\Xset(\ell(u^\star))$. For $\varphi\le1$ this is a nondecreasing transformation of $R$, and $\xi^\star$ maximizes $R$ over $\Xset(\ell(u^\star))$ by block optimality of the integrated optimum; hence no profitable deviation exists. \emph{$\W$'s side.} Given $\xi^\star$, a deviation $u'\in\Qset$ is available only if the operating point obtained by fixing $\E$'s decisions and letting the metered exchange adjust to $\ell(u')$ remains feasible; on that set the site's settlement is $R$ itself evaluated at a point feasible for \eqref{eq:milp}, so $R(u',\xi')\le\Pi^\star=R(u^\star,\xi^\star)$. $\W$'s payoff change is $\varphi\big[R(u',\xi')-R(u^\star,\xi^\star)\big]\le0$ for every $\varphi\ge0$, so no profitable deviation exists, proving (i). For (ii), transfers cancel in the sum, $\Pi_{\W}+\Pi_{\E}=\Pi^\star$; for any target division $(a,\Pi^\star-a)$ choose any $\varphi\in[0,1]$ and $F=\varphi\Pi^\star-a$. Nothing in the argument uses convexity of $\Qset$ or $\Xset$. \hfill$\blacksquare$

\subsection{Proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:window}}
$\W$ is no worse off than in the baseline iff $\varphi R^\star-F\ge-\bill^0$, i.e., $F\le\bill^0+\varphi R^\star$; $\E$ iff $(1-\varphi)R^\star+F\ge R^0+\bill^0$, i.e., $F\ge\bill^0+R^0-(1-\varphi)R^\star$. The interval is nonempty because its width is $\varphi R^\star+(1-\varphi)R^\star-R^0=\gain\ge0$. Substituting $F=\bill^0+\varphi R^0$ gives $\Pi_{\W}=\varphi(R^\star-R^0)-\bill^0=-\bill^0+\varphi\gain$ and $\Pi_{\E}=R^\star-\varphi R^\star+\bill^0+\varphi R^0=R^0+\bill^0+(1-\varphi)\gain$; the anchored fee lies in the window because $R^0\le R^\star$. With fallbacks at the baseline payoffs, the Nash bargaining solution maximizes $(\varphi\gain)((1-\varphi)\gain)$, attained at $\varphi=1/2$. \hfill$\blacksquare$

\subsection{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:price}}
With the binaries fixed, \eqref{eq:milp} is an LP in which the pump load enters only the right-hand side of the nodal balance \eqref{eq:e_balance} at the pump buses; by LP sensitivity its multiplier $\lambda_{b,t}$ is the marginal cost of an additional kilowatt of load there, and it is also the multiplier of the relaxed interface \eqref{eq:c_pumpload}, which is the internal price. (i) At a PCC bus with a slack import rating and $y^{\mathrm{g}}=1$, stationarity in $p^{\mathrm{g}}_{b,t}$ gives $\lambda_{b,t}=c^{\mathrm{buy}}_t$ when the import is strictly positive (its lower bound is slack); symmetrically $\lambda_{b,t}=c^{\mathrm{sell}}_t$ in an export hour with a slack export rating. In an idle hour both variables sit at their lower bound, so stationarity yields $c^{\mathrm{sell}}_t\le\lambda_{b,t}\le c^{\mathrm{buy}}_t$; the value within the band is determined by the stationarity conditions of the battery variables that are strictly between their bounds, i.e., by the intertemporal arbitrage. (ii) A binding import rating adds its nonnegative multiplier to $c^{\mathrm{buy}}_t$; a binding export rating subtracts one from $c^{\mathrm{sell}}_t$. If PV is curtailed in hour $t$, $p^{\mathrm{pv}}_{b,t}$ is strictly inside its bounds, and stationarity in it gives $\lambda_{b,t}=0$ at its bus. (iii) The lossless linearized flows make the nodal balances of a connected feeder sum to the PCC balance with the line flows cancelling; with no voltage or current limit binding, the line-flow, voltage, and angle variables are unconstrained beyond \eqref{eq:e_pflow}--\eqref{eq:e_qflow}, and stationarity in them forces all $\lambda_{b,t}$ to coincide; a binding limit on a line introduces its multiplier as the difference between the two end buses. \hfill$\blacksquare$

\subsection{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:convergence}}
$D$ is a minimum of finitely many affine functions of $\pi$, one for each pair of an integer assignment in $\Qset$ and a vertex of the corresponding polyhedron in $\Xset$, hence concave and piecewise linear; weak duality gives $D(\pi)\le C^\star$ for every $\pi$. (i) Each cut is an affine majorant of $D$ that is exact at the price where it was generated; the bundle rule with serious and null steps on a polyhedral concave function terminates finitely at a maximizer \cite{lemarechal2001}, and inexact subproblem values shift each cut by at most the subproblem tolerance, so the certified bound, computed from the solvers' proven bounds, lies within that tolerance of $D^\star$. (ii) is the standard convergence of the projected subgradient method with diminishing steps for concave functions with bounded supergradients \cite{bertsekas1999}. (iii) The metered schedule is feasible for $\W$ by construction and the response is feasible for $\E$ by Assumption~\ref{ass:adequacy}, so their value is the cost of a feasible point of \eqref{eq:milp}, and the incumbent is within the certified gap of $C^\star$. (iv) By the Geoffrion characterization, $D^\star$ equals the value of \eqref{eq:milp} with $\Qset$ and $\Xset$ replaced by their convex hulls, so the gap vanishes iff the integer optimum is also optimal for that convexified problem. (v) The message count is read off Algorithm~\ref{alg:coordination}: one vector $\pi^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\Bset_{\Pset}|T}$ and one vector $\ell^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\Bset_{\Pset}|T}$ per iteration; the master problem is built from those vectors and $\E$'s own subproblems. \hfill$\blacksquare$
